q: Which of the following culture-bound syndromes is NOT reported in India?
who: Latah, a Malaysian and Indonesian culture-bound syndrome

concept.t: Latah is an exaggerated startle with echolalia, echopraxia, automatic obedience and blurted obscenities.
It belongs to Malaysia and Indonesia, not India, so it is the syndrome not reported here.

wrong.a: Reported in India: anxiety over semen loss.
wrong.b: Reported in India: fear that the genitals are retracting, with epidemics in north-east India.
wrong.c: Reported in India: obsessional cleanliness in Bengal.

q: The diathesis-stress model of psychopathology suggests that mental disorders result from:

concept.t: The diathesis is a genetic, biological or psychological vulnerability. It produces disorder only when a stressor sets it off.
Zubin and Spring (1977) called this the vulnerability-stress model.
Every option ending in 'only' names a single cause, the one-dimensional thinking the model replaced.

wrong.a: Names a single cause; genes can be the diathesis, but without a stressor the model predicts no disorder.
wrong.b: Names a single cause; a stressor needs an existing vulnerability to set off.
wrong.d: Names a single cause; a biological abnormality is one kind of diathesis, which still needs a stressor.

q: A high false positive rate in diagnosis means:

concept.t: A false positive wrongly labels a healthy person as ill.
It happens when diagnostic criteria are too loose, so normal people get swept in.

wrong.a: Over-strict criteria cause the opposite error, false negatives, where real cases are missed.
wrong.c: Low reliability means clinicians disagree with each other, a separate problem.
wrong.d: These are false negatives, the result of over-strict criteria.

q: Hypnagogic hallucinations most commonly occur in:
who: Hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucinations as normal experience

concept.t: Hypnagogic hallucinations occur while falling asleep; hypnopompic ones occur on waking.
They lie within normal experience and are commonest in healthy people. Narcolepsy also features them.

wrong.a: The hallucinations of schizophrenia are mainly auditory and occur in clear consciousness.
wrong.b: Delirium brings visual and tactile hallucinations; hypnagogic ones are still commonest in healthy people.
wrong.c: Drugs bring visual and tactile hallucinations; hypnagogic ones are still commonest in healthy people.

q: Our current mood and feelings are best described by the term:

concept.t: Affect is the immediate, observed, moment-to-moment expression of emotion: the weather.
Mood is the sustained state the person reports: the climate.

wrong.a: The broader term for a brief reaction, not the observed moment-to-moment expression.
wrong.b: The sustained state the person reports (the climate), not the current moment.
wrong.d: The experienced side of an emotion, not its observed expression.

q: Choose the correct arrangement of these stages of elevated mood based upon severity: i) Elation, ii) Exaltation, iii) Euphoria, iv) Ecstasy.
who: Grades of elevated mood, euphoria to ecstasy

concept.t: Elevated mood rises from euphoria (mild; hypomania) through elation (moderate; mania).
Next comes exaltation (intense, with grandiosity; severe mania), then ecstasy (rapture; stuporous or delirious mania).
So the order is iii (euphoria), i (elation), ii (exaltation), iv (ecstasy).

wrong.a: Puts elation first, but euphoria is the mildest grade.
wrong.c: Reverses the scale, putting ecstasy, the most severe grade, first.
wrong.d: Fails because option (b) gives the correct order.

q: Which is NOT a core symptom to diagnose as autism in children as per DSM- 5?

concept.t: DSM-5 autism rests on two core domains: social communication and reciprocity, and restricted, repetitive behaviour.
Intellectual impairment is only a specifier (with or without), not a core symptom.

wrong.a: Core: part of the social communication domain.
wrong.b: Core: the restricted, repetitive behaviour domain.
wrong.c: Core: part of the social communication and reciprocity domain.

q: In which of the following situations would a diagnosis of "global developmental delay" be inappropriate?
who: Global developmental delay, provisional label under age 5

concept.t: Global developmental delay is a provisional label for children under 5 whose severity cannot yet be reliably assessed.
A testable 7-year-old who meets both criteria (IQ 65, severe adaptive impairment) has intellectual disability, so the provisional label does not fit.

wrong.a: Appropriate: a child too young to be assessed is exactly the provisional case the label exists for.
wrong.c: Appropriate: without adaptive data, severity cannot yet be reliably assessed.
wrong.d: Appropriate: without standardised cognitive testing, severity cannot yet be reliably assessed.

q: Within attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, which of the following is NOT classified as a problem relating to hyperactivity/impulsivity?

concept.t: ADHD symptoms fall into two lists: inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity.
Not seeming to listen when spoken to directly is one of the nine inattention items, so it is not a hyperactivity-impulsivity problem.

wrong.a: A hyperactivity-impulsivity item, so it does belong on that list.
wrong.b: A hyperactivity-impulsivity item (squirming and fidgeting), so it belongs on that list.
wrong.c: A hyperactivity-impulsivity item, so it belongs on that list.

q: "First rank symptoms" of schizophrenia given by Schneider include all except

concept.t: Kurt Schneider listed first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia, including running-commentary voices, delusional perception and thought broadcasting.
Depersonalisation, like loose associations and delusions of self-reference, is not a first-rank symptom.

wrong.b: On Schneider's list: one of his first-rank auditory hallucinations.
wrong.c: On Schneider's list: a normal perception suddenly given a delusional meaning.
wrong.d: On Schneider's list: the belief that one's thoughts are being made known to others.

q: The ICD-10 duration criterion for schizophrenia requires symptoms to persist for at least:
who: ICD-10 and ICD-11 schizophrenia duration criterion

concept.t: ICD-10 and ICD-11 require schizophrenia symptoms to last at least 1 month.
DSM-5-TR uses a longer total of six months instead, so the two systems differ.

wrong.a: The DSM-5-TR total, including 1 month of active-phase symptoms, not the ICD figure.
wrong.b: The 2-week onset window of acute and transient psychotic disorders, not schizophrenia.
wrong.c: Matches neither system: ICD needs 1 month, DSM-5-TR 6 months in total.

q: High EE (Expressed Emotion) is known to cause:
who: Brown, Birley and Wing (1972); Vaughn and Leff (1976)

concept.t: Expressed emotion (EE) means critical, hostile or over-involved attitudes in a patient's relatives.
Brown, Birley and Wing (1972) and Vaughn and Leff (1976) showed that such relatives predict relapse after discharge.

wrong.a: Too vague: the research finding is specifically relapse after discharge, the better answer.
wrong.c: EE does not cause the illness or its negative symptoms; it predicts relapse.
wrong.d: EE does not cause violence; its established link is with relapse.

q: Which of the following statements concerning Bipolar disorder is INCORRECT?
who: Bipolar I versus bipolar II definitions

concept.t: Bipolar I is defined by at least one manic episode; hypomania is optional in it.
Hypomania is the defining high of bipolar II, so claiming it as a bipolar I feature is the incorrect statement.

wrong.a: True: at least one manic episode defines bipolar I.
wrong.b: True: hypomania is the defining high of bipolar II.
wrong.d: True: bipolar I may include depressive periods, even below the major depressive threshold.

q: A 12-year-old boy begins to have new episodes of temper outbursts that are out of proportion to the situation. Which of the following is NOT a diagnostic possibility in this patient?

concept.t: DMDD requires onset before age 10, with diagnosis made between 6 and 18.
Outbursts that begin at 12 rule it out, so DMDD is not a possibility here.

wrong.b: Possible: bipolar disorder can begin or present at this age.
wrong.c: Possible: conduct disorder can begin or present at this age.
wrong.d: Possible: ADHD can present at this age.

q: Suicidal risk is assessed to be highest when the following criteria are met in comparison to others, the 'time' factor being the same for all

concept.t: Risk is highest when several markers converge.
A highly lethal method, a specific plan, frequent ideation and a family history of suicide.

wrong.b: Lacks ideation and a recent attempt, so the key markers are missing.
wrong.c: Lacks a previous attempt, and intent is only moderate.
wrong.d: Has low lethality and no family history, so fewer markers converge despite the recent attempt.

q: The following defense mechanisms are used in obsessive-compulsive disorder:
who: Classic OCD defences, undoing as the key

concept.t: Isolation, undoing and reaction formation are all classic OCD defences.
Undoing, an act that symbolically cancels a forbidden thought, is the most characteristic, so it is the key.

wrong.a: A classic OCD defence too (cutting a thought off from its feeling), but less characteristic than undoing.
wrong.c: Also a classic OCD defence (acting opposite to an unacceptable impulse), but undoing is the most characteristic.
wrong.d: The defence of phobias, as in Freud's Little Hans case.

q: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a pervasive condition in which the sufferer experiences:

concept.t: GAD is excessive, hard-to-control, free-floating worry about many matters.
The worry must last at least 6 months.

wrong.b: Fear of fear marks panic disorder and agoraphobia, not GAD.
wrong.c: Flashbacks mark PTSD, not GAD.
wrong.d: Checking marks OCD, not GAD.

q: A client with OCD washes their hands excessively to neutralize the anxiety caused by intrusive thoughts of contamination. This hand-washing behavior is BEST conceptualized as a(n):

concept.t: In Mowrer's two-factor account, fear is learned by classical conditioning and kept going by avoidance.
The washing removes anxiety, so it is negatively reinforced: an avoidance response or safety behaviour.

wrong.a: The contamination thought is the conditioned stimulus; the washing is the response to it.
wrong.b: An unconditioned response is an unlearned reflex; hand-washing is learned.
wrong.d: Nothing pleasant is added; anxiety is removed, so it is negative, not positive, reinforcement.

q: The term 'la Bella indifference' seen in hysteria was first used by:

concept.t: La belle indifférence is the calm unconcern some conversion patients show about their symptoms.
The phrase is usually credited to Pierre Janet, who explained hysteria as dissociation.

wrong.a: Freud explained hysteria by repression and conversion; the phrase is usually credited to Janet.
wrong.b: Anna Freud catalogued the defences, not hysterical unconcern.
wrong.d: Hippocrates blamed hysteria on a wandering womb.

q: When an individual has dissociative amnesia it is usually associated with several types of memory disturbances. In contrast, in generalized amnesia:

concept.t: Generalised amnesia covers the whole life history, often with identity.
Loss of a set period is localised amnesia; loss of one category of information is systematised.

wrong.a: Loss of a set period such as a week is localised amnesia.
wrong.c: Covers only one period, not the whole life history, so it is not generalised.
wrong.d: Describes dissociative amnesia in general, not the generalised type.

q: The difference between malingering and factitious disorder lies in:
who: Malingering versus factitious disorder: external incentive

concept.t: In both malingering and factitious disorder people deliberately falsify symptoms and know they are false.
The malingerer seeks an external incentive such as money or escape from duty. Factitious disorder persists without obvious external reward, to occupy the sick role.

wrong.b: Both know their symptoms are false, so belief does not separate them.
wrong.c: Not the distinguishing feature; the difference is whether an external reward is sought.
wrong.d: Not the distinguishing feature; what separates them is motive, external reward or the sick role.

q: Unlike people with anorexia, individuals with bulimia
who: Anorexia nervosa criterion: significantly low body weight

concept.t: Significantly low body weight is a criterion of anorexia nervosa.
People with bulimia are usually of normal weight or overweight.

wrong.a: Purging occurs in both: the binge-eating/purging type of anorexia purges too.
wrong.b: Fear of fatness occurs in both disorders, so it does not distinguish them.
wrong.c: Damage to health occurs in both disorders, so it does not distinguish them.

q: In narcolepsy, which of the following is most characteristically present?

concept.t: Cataplexy is brief, sudden, bilateral loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness, triggered by laughter or joking.
It marks narcolepsy type 1, caused by loss of hypocretin (orexin) neurons.

wrong.a: Fails: catalepsy belongs to catatonia, not narcolepsy.
wrong.c: Fails: cataplexy is the characteristic feature of narcolepsy type 1.
wrong.d: Catalepsy, a held posture with waxy flexibility, belongs to catatonia.

q: Lack of bowel control in children is known as:

concept.t: Encopresis is repeated passage of faeces into inappropriate places.
It must happen at least once a month for 3 months, from age 4.

wrong.b: Not a recognised elimination disorder.
wrong.c: The urinary counterpart of encopresis, diagnosed from age 5.
wrong.d: An eating disorder, not an elimination disorder.

q: Premature ejaculation is most commonly associated with:

concept.t: Premature ejaculation is mostly psychogenic and most tied to performance anxiety.
It is commoner in men with anxiety disorders.

wrong.a: Diabetes is the classic link of erectile disorder, not premature ejaculation.
wrong.b: A myth: masturbation does not cause it.
wrong.c: Personality disorder has no special association with it.

q: Autogynephilia is defined by:

concept.t: Autogynephilia is sexual attraction to thoughts or images of oneself as a woman.
Ray Blanchard coined the term in 1989, and DSM-5-TR uses it as a specifier of transvestic disorder.

wrong.a: Defines pedophilia, not autogynephilia.
wrong.c: Mere attraction to oneself is not autogynephilia; the term needs the image of oneself as a woman.
wrong.d: Defines masochism, not autogynephilia.

q: When gender incongruence moved out of the mental disorders chapter in ICD-11, which of these stayed in Chapter 6 (Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders)?

concept.t: ICD-11 moved gender incongruence (of childhood as well as of adolescence or adulthood), the sexual dysfunctions and the sexual pain disorders into Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health.
Only the paraphilic disorders, now centred on non-consent, stayed in Chapter 6.

wrong.a: Moved to Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health.
wrong.c: Moved to Chapter 17 along with the sexual dysfunctions.
wrong.d: Moved to Chapter 17, along with gender incongruence of adolescence or adulthood.

q: A patient presents with severe memory deficits, confabulation, and nystagmus, with a history of chronic alcohol use. This clinical picture is classic for:

concept.t: Thiamine deficiency in chronic drinkers damages the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus.
Nystagmus belongs to Wernicke's encephalopathy; amnesia with confabulation to Korsakoff's syndrome.

wrong.a: Gradual memory decline from plaques and tangles; not caused by alcohol and does not produce this triad.
wrong.c: Decline after strokes or small-vessel disease; not caused by alcohol and does not produce this triad.
wrong.d: Early change in personality and behaviour; not caused by alcohol and does not produce this triad.

q: Which of the following substances is NOT a natural alkaloid compound?

concept.t: Heroin (diacetylmorphine) is made by chemically modifying morphine, so it is semi-synthetic.
Morphine, codeine and papaverine all occur naturally in opium.

wrong.a: A natural opium alkaloid, and the starting material for heroin.
wrong.c: A natural opium alkaloid.
wrong.d: A natural opium alkaloid, though a smooth-muscle relaxant rather than a narcotic.

q: A key of distinguishing feature of dementia vs. delirium is :

concept.t: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness.
Dementia is an insidious decline in memory and cognition in clear consciousness.

wrong.a: Delusions occur in both, so they do not distinguish them.
wrong.b: Reverses the two onsets: delirium is acute, dementia insidious.
wrong.c: Hallucinations occur in both, so they do not distinguish them.

q: Borderline Personality Disorder is most characteristically associated with which primary defense mechanism?

concept.t: Splitting means seeing self and others as all good or all bad.
Kernberg placed this primitive defence at the centre of borderline personality organisation.

wrong.a: The classic neurotic defence; it does not define BPD.
wrong.c: A mature defence; it does not define BPD.
wrong.d: Means giving a plausible excuse; it does not define BPD.

q: Identify the 'odd one out' from the groups:
who: Personality disorder clusters A and B

concept.t: Paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal form Cluster A (odd or eccentric).
Borderline belongs to Cluster B (dramatic, emotional or erratic).

wrong.a: Cluster A (odd or eccentric), with schizoid and schizotypal.
wrong.b: Cluster A, with paranoid and schizotypal.
wrong.c: Cluster A, with paranoid and schizoid.

q: A client reports a persistent pattern of seeking admiration, but their behavior is characterized by excessive emotionality, attention-seeking, and seductive behavior, rather than grandiosity. This presentation is more characteristic of:

concept.t: Excessive emotionality, attention seeking and seductive behaviour define histrionic PD.
Narcissistic PD also seeks admiration, but rests on grandiosity, which this client lacks.

wrong.a: Also seeks admiration, but rests on grandiosity and lack of empathy, absent here.
wrong.c: Centres on instability and fear of abandonment.
wrong.d: Centres on a need to be taken care of.
